newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans vote for change in key elections.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans vote for change in key elections.

text.p: Mexicans voted on Sunday in key local elections in three states, with many voters expected to punish President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) by choosing the opposition.

Still reeling from Mexico's worst economic crisis in 60 years and angered by successive corruption scandals, voters interviewed at random in the Mexico state municipality of Naucalpan said it was time to end the PRI's reign there.

"Lots of people don't want to vote for the PRI because they are ruining the country. Look at the number of houses for sale round here," said voter Gerardo Vasquez as he stepped out of a polling station.
The PRI has ruled Mexico's federal government without a break for 67 years and until recently opposition parties barely had any representation at all in town halls, state governorships or Congress.

Voting began in cold winter weather at 8 a.m. local time (1400 GMT) though radio reports said late delivery of electoral materials and the absence of key officials had delayed the opening of some polling stations.
Results were due to start trickling in late on Sunday night, with a clear tendency likely to be established by dawn on Monday.

Of the three states voting on Sunday, the most important was the state of Mexico, the heartland of the old Aztec empire, which straggles around Mexico City to the north, east and west. Home to 11.7 million people, the state is the country's most populous and home to much of its industry.

Opinion polls suggested a tight, three-way fight for Mexico state's top five municipalities among the PRI and its two main rivals, the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).
Naucalpan, which is part of the sprawl of greater Mexico City, is the state's third biggest municipality and the PAN had high hopes of capturing it.
"I hope the PAN wins," said voter Pedro Moreno. "But we say that every time and yet the PRI always wins."

Several voters complained of the PRI's lavish election propaganda in Naucalpan, which included large aluminium-framed boxes tied to lampposts carrying an illuminated poster for their candidate Roberto Flores -- lit up with electricity tapped from the public supply.

"We want people who will govern us with honesty and common sense," said Enrique Perez, another voter. "The last four presidents we had left the country in ruins. They say they stole $87 billion between them."

All three parties were treating the elections as a dry run for key midterm congressional votes next July -- a date which will also see the first-ever election of a mayor of Mexico City. Hitherto the post was held by presidential appointees.

Sunday's elections, which also included the northern state of Coahuila bordering Texas and the poor central state of Hidalgo, provided a test of Zedillo's commitment to cleaning up Mexico's historically dubious electoral record.
Allegations of PRI fraud have scarred many of the governing party's victories in recent years and Zedillo was determined to show his country could hold clean elections.

To prevent fraud, voters were to use a electoral photo-ID card, which officials at the polling station would check against a voter list printed on security paper that includes a photo of every citizen registered.
The greater precautions were to little avail in Coahuila state, where both the PRI and the PAN accused each other of dirty tricks long before voting began.
In Hidalgo, a poor former silver-mining state which borders the state of Mexico to the northeast, the electoral temperature appeared to be lower.

As in many of Mexico's poorer and more backward states, the PRI's main challenge in Hidalgo was coming not from the PAN but from the left-wing PRD, which hoped to capture some of the state's larger town halls. The opposition currently holds just one municipality out of 84 in that state.
